## Ranked search

Pass a `search` object to rank companies against a natural-language query.
`search.query` is required and must not be empty. `search.mode` controls which
retrieval methods run.

| Mode | Keyword retrieval | Semantic retrieval | When to use |
| - | - | - | - |
| `hybrid` | Yes | Yes | Most discovery queries. This is the default. |
| `lexical` | Yes | No | Queries where matching the supplied words matters most. |
| `semantic` | No | Yes | Conceptual queries that may use different wording from descriptions. |

When you supply `filters`, the API applies them as hard constraints before
keyword or semantic retrieval. Ranked results are ordered by relevance, so you
cannot combine `search` with `sorts`. Ranked search returns up to 100 results
per page and supports cursors across at most 1,000 candidate positions per search.

```json theme={"theme":"vitesse-black"}
{
    "search": {
        "query": "developer tooling companies building observability products",
        "mode": "hybrid"
    },
    "filters": {
        "field": "locations.country",
        "type": "=",
        "value": "USA"
    },
    "limit": 20
}
```

***

## Filter operator reference

Company Search accepts the following `filters.type` operators.

| Operator | Value shape | Meaning | Example value | Notes |
| - | - | - | - | - |
| `=` | scalar | Exact match | `"retool.com"` | Case-insensitive for text fields |
| `!=` | scalar | Not equal | `"acquired"` | |
| `<` | scalar (number or date string) | Less than | `10000` | Numbers and date strings |
| `=<` | scalar (number or date string) | Less than or equal | `50000000` | **Not** `<=` |
| `>` | scalar (number or date string) | Greater than | `2020` | Numbers and date strings |
| `=>` | scalar (number or date string) | Greater than or equal | `"2024-01-01"` | **Not** `>=` |
| `in` | array | Value is in list | `["USA", "GBR"]` | Case-insensitive for text fields when the list has 100 values or fewer. A longer list is case-sensitive. Matches if **any** array element matches **any** list value. |
| `not_in` | array | Value is not in list | `["acquired"]` | Same case rule as `in`. |
| `is_null` | `null` | Field has no value | `null` | The `value` key is required. Send `"value": null`. |
| `is_not_null` | `null` | Field has a non-null value | `null` | The `value` key is required. Send `"value": null`. |
| `(.)` | string | Fuzzy all-words match | `"Software Development"` | Every query word must match a word in the value, in any order, and typos are tolerated. Matches "Development Software" and "Sftware Devlpment", not ~~"Software Dev"~~. |
| `[.]` | string | Case-insensitive exact-phrase match | `"Software Development"` | `[.]` "Software Development" matches "Software Development Platform", not ~~"Development Software"~~. Words must be contiguous and in order, with no partial words or typos. |
| `geo_distance` | object | HQ within radius of a location or explicit coordinate | `{"location": "Palo Alto, CA", "distance": 50, "unit": "km"}` | Only on `locations.headquarters`. See [`geo_distance`](#geo_distance--radius-around-headquarters) |
| `geo_exclude` | object | HQ outside radius of a location or explicit coordinate | `{"location": "London, UK", "distance": 100, "unit": "km"}` | Inverse of `geo_distance`, with the same value object and field. See [`geo_exclude`](#geo_exclude--exclude-a-radius) |
| `geo_polygon` | object | HQ inside a polygon of explicit coordinates | `{"points": [[37.8, -122.5], [37.8, -122.3], [37.6, -122.4]]}` | Same field as `geo_distance`. See [`geo_polygon`](#geo_polygon-inside-a-polygon) |

> [!WARNING]
>
> The operators `>=` and `<=` are **not supported**. Use `=>` and `=<`
> instead.

> [!NOTE]
>
> To require two values on a list field, such as `basic_info.industries`,
> put two `=` conditions in an `and` group. The API returns the companies
> whose list holds both values. `has_all` returns `400` on
> `basic_info.industries` and `taxonomy.professional_network_industry`.

### `geo_distance` — radius around headquarters

`geo_distance` keeps companies whose **headquarters** is within a radius of a
point. All three geo operators work on the `locations.headquarters` field only.
Supply the centre of the radius using **one** of:

* `location` — a string that is geocoded server-side (e.g. `"Palo Alto, CA"`).
* `lat_lng` — explicit coordinates as `[lat, lng]`. Skips geocoding.

If both are supplied, `lat_lng` wins. `distance` is required; `unit` defaults
to `km`.

| Field | Type | Required | Notes |
| - | - | - | - |
| `location` | string | One of | Geocoded server-side. Ignored when `lat_lng` is also set. |
| `lat_lng` | number\[] | One of | Two-element `[lat, lng]`. Lat in `[-90, 90]`, lng in `[-180, 180]`. |
| `distance` | number | Yes | Radius around the centre. Must be positive. |
| `unit` | string | No | One of `km`, `mi`, `miles`, `m`, `meters`, `ft`, `feet`. Defaults to `km`. |

See [`geo_distance` examples](/company-docs/search/introduction#examples)
for end-to-end requests using both `location` and `lat_lng`.

### `geo_exclude` — exclude a radius

`geo_exclude` is the inverse of `geo_distance`: it removes companies
headquartered **inside** the radius and keeps everyone else. It takes the same
value object — `location` or `lat_lng`, a required `distance`, and an optional
`unit` (defaults to `km`) — and works on the same `locations.headquarters`
field. Use it to carve out a metro you already cover, or to target companies
outside a region.

```json theme={"theme":"vitesse-black"}
{
    "field": "locations.headquarters",
    "type": "geo_exclude",
    "value": { "location": "London, UK", "distance": 100, "unit": "km" }
}
```

### `geo_polygon`: inside a polygon

`geo_polygon` keeps companies whose **headquarters** falls inside a polygon you
draw with explicit coordinates. Use it when a radius is the wrong shape: a
sales territory, a metro boundary, or an area you traced on a map. It works on
the same `locations.headquarters` field as `geo_distance`.

| Field | Type | Required | Notes |
| - | - | - | - |
| `points` | number\[]\[] | Yes | List of `[lat, lng]` pairs, at least 3 distinct points and at most 1,000. Lat in `[-90, 90]`, lng in `[-180, 180]`. |

The polygon closes itself, so repeating the first point is optional. Edges may
not cross, and no point may be revisited. Points are coordinates, not place
names, and are not geocoded. A polygon that crosses the 180° meridian must
list its points counter-clockwise, or it is read as everything outside it.

```json theme={"theme":"vitesse-black"}
{
    "field": "locations.headquarters",
    "type": "geo_polygon",
    "value": { "points": [[37.8, -122.5], [37.8, -122.3], [37.6, -122.4]] }
}
```

A polygon with fewer than 3 distinct points, a malformed pair, crossing edges,
or an out-of-range coordinate returns `400` with a message naming the problem,
for example `geo_polygon 'points' needs at least 3 distinct points`.

## Searchable fields

These are common fields that can be used in the `field` key of a filter condition. Some indexed filter fields are search-only and are not returned in the response payload. For the full schema, see the [API reference](/openapi-specs/2025-11-01/introduction).

Fields are grouped by family below. Every field listed is filterable; the **Sortable** column marks the subset also valid in `sorts`.

### Identity & timestamps

| Field | Type | Filterable | Sortable | Description |
| - | - | - | - | - |
| `crustdata_company_id` | integer | Yes | Yes | Crustdata company ID |
| `basic_info.company_id` | integer | Yes | Yes | Internal source company ID |
| `metadata.growth_calculation_date` | datetime | Yes | Yes | Anchor date for growth metrics |
| `updated_at` | datetime | Yes | Yes | Last profile update timestamp |
| `indexed_at` | datetime | Yes | Yes | Last index timestamp |

### Basic info

| Field | Type | Filterable | Sortable | Description |
| - | - | - | - | - |
| `basic_info.name` | string | Yes | Yes | Company name |
| `basic_info.primary_domain` | string | Yes | Yes | Primary website domain |
| `basic_info.website` | string | Yes | No | Full website URL |
| `basic_info.professional_network_url` | string | Yes | No | Company profile URL |
| `basic_info.professional_network_id` | string | Yes | No | Company profile ID |
| `basic_info.company_type` | string | Yes | No | e.g., `"Privately Held"`, `"Public Company"` |
| `basic_info.status` | string | Yes | No | Company lifecycle: `"active"` or `"deleted"` |
| `basic_info.year_founded` | integer | Yes | Yes | Year founded (e.g., `2017`) |
| `basic_info.employee_count_range` | string | Yes | Yes | e.g., `"201-500"` |
| `basic_info.markets` | string\[] | Yes | No | Market tags |
| `basic_info.industries` | string\[] | Yes | No | Industry tags; filter alias of `taxonomy.professional_network_industries` |

> [!NOTE]
>
> **`basic_info.status`** is the company's lifecycle in Crustdata's entity
> graph. It is the same value the person APIs return as `company_status` on an
> employment record. Two values are defined:
>
> * `active`: a live company record.
> * `deleted`: a record Crustdata has retired. Other records can still point at
>   it, so you meet this value most often in a person's employment history.
>
> Company search serves the live company index, so a `deleted` company is not a
> result there. Filter `basic_info.status` when you want the check written into
> the query, and read it on the response to see the lifecycle of a company you
> already matched.

### Revenue & funding

| Field | Type | Filterable | Sortable | Description |
| - | - | - | - | - |
| `revenue.estimated.lower_bound_usd` | integer | Yes | Yes | Revenue lower bound (USD) |
| `revenue.estimated.upper_bound_usd` | integer | Yes | Yes | Revenue upper bound (USD) |
| `revenue.acquisition_status` | string | Yes | No | e.g., `"acquired"` |
| `revenue.public_markets.ipo_date` | date | Yes | Yes | IPO date (public companies) |
| `revenue.public_markets.fiscal_year_end` | string | Yes | No | Fiscal year end (public companies) |
| `revenue.public_markets.stock_symbols` | string\[] | Yes | No | Ticker symbols (public companies) |
| `funding.total_investment_usd` | number | Yes | Yes | Total disclosed funding (USD) |
| `funding.last_round_amount_usd` | number | Yes | Yes | Last funding round amount (USD) |
| `funding.last_fundraise_date` | date | Yes | Yes | Last funding date |
| `funding.last_round_type` | string | Yes | No | Latest round type, e.g., `"series_a"` |
| `funding.investors` | string\[] | Yes | No | All-time investor names; not round-specific |

### Headcount & roles

| Field | Type | Filterable | Sortable | Description |
| - | - | - | - | - |
| `headcount.total` | integer | Yes | Yes | Total employee count |
| `headcount.largest_headcount_country` | string | Yes | Yes | Country with the most employees |
| `headcount.growth_percent.1m` | number | Yes | No | 1-month headcount growth percent |
| `headcount.growth_percent.3m` | number | Yes | No | 3-month headcount growth percent |
| `headcount.growth_percent.6m` | number | Yes | No | 6-month headcount growth percent |
| `headcount.growth_percent.12m` | number | Yes | No | 12-month headcount growth percent |
| `headcount.growth_absolute.1m` | integer | Yes | No | 1-month absolute employee delta |
| `headcount.growth_absolute.3m` | integer | Yes | No | 3-month absolute employee delta |
| `headcount.growth_absolute.6m` | integer | Yes | No | 6-month absolute employee delta |
| `headcount.growth_absolute.12m` | integer | Yes | No | 12-month absolute employee delta |
| `roles.distribution.<function>` | integer | Yes | No | Employee count in a function (see list below) |
| `roles.distribution_percent` | object | Yes | No | Share of employees per function |
| `roles.growth_6m` | object | Yes | No | 6-month role growth |
| `roles.growth_yoy` | object | Yes | No | Year-over-year role growth |

> [!NOTE]
>
> The `headcount.growth_percent.*` and `headcount.growth_absolute.*` dotted
> period paths are **filterable but not sortable**. To rank results by growth,
> filter on the period you care about and sort on `headcount.total` (or
> another sortable field). See [Find high-growth mid-size
> companies](/company-docs/search/introduction#examples).

Replace `<function>` with one of: `accounting`, `administrative`, `arts_and_design`, `business_development`, `community_and_social_services`, `consulting`, `customer_success_and_support`, `education`, `engineering`, `entrepreneurship`, `finance`, `healthcare_services`, `human_resources`, `information_technology`, `legal`, `marketing`, `media_and_communication`, `military_and_protective_services`, `operations`, `product_management`, `program_and_project_management`, `purchasing`, `quality_assurance`, `real_estate`, `research`, `sales`, `support`. For example, `roles.distribution.engineering` filters on the number of engineers. See [Find companies by team size in a function](/company-docs/search/introduction#examples).

### Locations

| Field | Type | Filterable | Sortable | Description |
| - | - | - | - | - |
| `locations.country` | string | Yes | Yes | HQ country. Filter with ISO-3 codes or full names; returns the normalized full name |
| `locations.state` | string | Yes | No | HQ state / region, normalized (e.g. `"California"`) |
| `locations.city` | string | Yes | No | HQ city, normalized (e.g. `"Palo Alto"`) |
| `locations.headquarters` | string | Yes | No | Full HQ location string, also the target of `geo_distance`, `geo_exclude` and `geo_polygon` |
| `locations.street_address` | string | Yes | No | HQ street address (e.g. `"510 Townsend St."`) |
| `locations.all_office_addresses` | string\[] | Yes | No | All office addresses, HQ and non-HQ; match a city or region substring with `(.)` |

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Normalized location facets.** `locations.state` and `locations.city`
> filter against and return normalized values derived from geocoding each
> company's headquarters address — the value you see in a response is the
> value you filter with. `locations.country` **accepts both** vocabularies:
> ISO-3 codes (`"USA"`, `"GBR"`) and full country names (`"United States"`)
> each match all companies, so existing ISO-3 filters keep working unchanged.
> Responses return the normalized full country name. Use
> [Autocomplete](/company-docs/autocomplete/introduction) to discover indexed
> values before filtering.

### Taxonomy

| Field | Type | Filterable | Sortable | Description |
| - | - | - | - | - |
| `taxonomy.professional_network_industry` | string\[] | Yes | No | Industry labels. A filter matches any label, the same as `basic_info.industries`. The response returns only the primary label, as a string |
| `taxonomy.categories` | string\[] | Yes | No | Category tags |
| `taxonomy.professional_network_specialities` | string\[] | Yes | No | Speciality tags |
| `taxonomy.primary_naics_detail.naics_code` | string | Yes | No | Six-digit NAICS code, for example `"541511"` |
| `taxonomy.primary_naics_detail.sector` | string | Yes | No | NAICS sector, the two-digit level |
| `taxonomy.primary_naics_detail.sub_sector` | string | Yes | No | NAICS sub-sector, the three-digit level |
| `taxonomy.primary_naics_detail.industry_group` | string | Yes | No | NAICS industry group, the four-digit level |
| `taxonomy.primary_naics_detail.industry` | string | Yes | No | NAICS industry title, the six-digit level |
| `taxonomy.primary_naics_detail.year` | integer | Yes | No | NAICS edition year |
| `taxonomy.sic_detail_list.sic_code` | string | Yes | No | Four-digit SIC code, for example `"7372"` |
| `taxonomy.sic_detail_list.industry` | string | Yes | No | SIC industry title |
| `taxonomy.sic_detail_list.year` | integer | Yes | No | SIC edition year |

> [!NOTE]
>
> **NAICS and SIC.** A company has one primary NAICS classification and a
> list of SIC entries. Search returns both as part of the `taxonomy` group.
> You can also name `taxonomy.primary_naics_detail`,
> `taxonomy.sic_detail_list`, or any leaf under them in `fields`. They have
> no price of their own. Most companies carry no classification and return
> `null` for both.
>
> Two `taxonomy.sic_detail_list.sic_code` conditions under `and` match a
> company whose list holds both codes, even in different entries. `has_all`
> with the same two codes returns the same companies.
>
> Every indexed NAICS code comes from the 2022 edition, and every SIC code
> from the 1987 edition, so each `year` field holds one value today. The
> `year` fields are not sortable. A sort on one returns `400` with the
> message `Unsupported columns in conditions:     ['taxonomy.primary_naics_detail.year']`.

### Followers

| Field | Type | Filterable | Sortable | Description |
| - | - | - | - | - |
| `followers.count` | integer | Yes | Yes | Follower count |
| `followers.mom_percent` | number | Yes | No | Month-over-month follower growth % |
| `followers.qoq_percent` | number | Yes | No | Quarter-over-quarter growth % |
| `followers.six_months_growth_percent` | number | Yes | No | 6-month follower growth % |
| `followers.yoy_percent` | number | Yes | No | Year-over-year follower growth % |

### Social profiles

| Field | Type | Filterable | Sortable | Description |
| - | - | - | - | - |
| `social_profiles.twitter_url` | string | Yes | No | Company X/Twitter URL |
| `social_profiles.crunchbase.url` | string | Yes | No | Company Crunchbase URL |
| `social_profiles.crunchbase.uuid` | string | Yes | No | Company Crunchbase UUID |
| `social_profiles.professional_network` | string | Yes | No | Company profile URL |

### Competitors (filter-only)

| Field | Type | Filterable | Sortable | Description |
| - | - | - | - | - |
| `competitors.company_ids` | integer\[] | Yes | No | Competitor Crustdata IDs |
| `competitors.websites` | string\[] | Yes | No | Competitor domains |

### Technographics (filter-only)

| Field | Type | Filterable | Sortable | Description |
| - | - | - | - | - |
| `technographics.total_technologies` | integer | Yes | Yes | Number of detected technologies |
| `technographics.top_technologies` | string\[] | Yes | No | Most notable technology names |
| `technographics.technologies.name` | string\[] | Yes | No | Detected technology names |
| `technographics.technologies.category` | string\[] | Yes | No | Detected technology category slugs |
| `technographics.technologies.super_category` | string\[] | Yes | No | Detected technology super-category slugs |

> [!NOTE]
>
> Technographics values are **not returned** in search responses. These
> fields are filter-only. `technographics.total_technologies` is filterable
> and sortable, but it is **not returned** in results.
> `technographics.top_technologies` is filterable but likewise not returned.
> `technographics.technologies.name` is likewise not returned, and
> `technographics.technologies.category` and
> `technographics.technologies.super_category` are likewise not returned. To
> get the values, request the `technographics` field group on [Company
> Enrich](/company-docs/enrichment/reference#technographics-fields). Use
> [Autocomplete](/company-docs/autocomplete/introduction#common-fields-to-autocomplete)
> with the `technology` and `technology_category` fields to discover valid
> filter values.

> [!TIP]
>
> Use [Autocomplete](/company-docs/autocomplete/introduction) to discover
> exact values for fields like `basic_info.industries`,
> `taxonomy.professional_network_industry`, `locations.country`,
> `basic_info.company_type`, and `funding.last_round_type`.

## Response fields

Each company in the response has `crustdata_company_id`, even when you do not request it. It can also include these sections, depending on `fields`. A section you request that has no data for the company is `null`.

| Section | Key fields | Description |
| - | - | - |
| `basic_info` | `name`, `primary_domain`, `website`, `professional_network_url`, `year_founded`, `status` | Core identity and profile |
| `headcount` | `total` | Employee footprint |
| `funding` | `total_investment_usd`, `last_round_amount_usd`, `investors` | Funding and investor data |
| `locations` | `country`, `state`, `city`, `headquarters`, `street_address`, `all_office_addresses` | Headquarters and office locations, with `country`, `state`, and `city` normalized as geocoded values |
| `taxonomy` | `professional_network_industry`, `professional_network_industries`, `categories`, `professional_network_specialities`, `primary_naics_detail`, `sic_detail_list` | Industry and category tags, plus the primary NAICS classification and the SIC entries |
| `revenue` | `estimated`, `public_markets`, `acquisition_status` | Revenue and market data |
| `hiring` | `openings_count`, `openings_growth_percent` | Hiring demand |
| `followers` | `count`, `mom_percent`, `yoy_percent` | Social follower metrics |
| `social_profiles` | `twitter_url`, `professional_network`, `crunchbase.url`, `crunchbase.uuid` | Third-party profile links |
| `software_reviews` | `average_rating`, `review_count`, and review-count growth percentages | Software review metrics (when available) |

### Filterable but not returned

Some indexed fields can be used in `filters` to narrow results but are **not**
part of the response payload — search is lightweight discovery, not full
enrichment. Filter on them, then fetch their values with
[Company Enrich](/company-docs/enrichment/introduction).

| Field family | Filterable | Returned |
| - | - | - |
| `basic_info.industries` (returned as `taxonomy.professional_network_industries`) | Yes | No |
| `competitors.*` (`company_ids`, `websites`) | Yes | No |
| `roles.*` (`distribution.<function>`, `distribution_percent`, `growth_6m`, `growth_yoy`) | Yes | No |
| `technographics.*` (`total_technologies`, `top_technologies`, `technologies.name`, `technologies.category`, `technologies.super_category`) | Yes | No |

***

## Validation rules

> [!NOTE]
>
> Default/max limits and pagination behavior reflect current platform
> behavior. See the [API reference](/openapi-specs/2025-11-01/introduction)
> for the formal OpenAPI contract.

| Rule | Behavior |
| - | - |
| Request criteria | Supply at least one of `filters` or `search`. |
| `search.query` | Required and non-empty when `search` is present. |
| `search.mode` | One of `hybrid`, `lexical`, or `semantic`. Defaults to `hybrid`. |
| `fields` is optional | Omitting returns all fields (large payload). Always specify in production. |
| Filter-only `limit` | 1 to 1000. Default: 20. |
| Ranked-search `limit` | 1 to 100. Default: 20. |
| Ranked search with `sorts` | Not supported. Ranked results preserve relevance order. |
| Ranked search with `cursor` | Supported in all three modes. See [ranked pagination](#ranked-pagination). |
| `sorts` with pagination | For filter-only search, include `sorts` when paginating to ensure stable result ordering. |
| `cursor` must match query | For filter-only search, changing `filters`, `sorts`, or `fields` between pages invalidates it. |

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Filter sizing.** To match many values of a field, put them all in a single
> `in` condition rather than many separate conditions — `in` compiles to one
> efficient query. A single `in` list of up to \~5,000-10,000 values returns in
> a few seconds; larger lists get progressively slower, and very large lists
> (roughly 50,000+) are rejected. For bigger sets, split the values into
> \~5,000-10,000 chunks across multiple requests and merge. The request body is
> hard-capped at **10 MB** (larger bodies return `413 request_too_large`),
> though with typical payloads you reach the query-size limit first.

## Errors

Common error responses for Search:

### Ranked cursor errors

A malformed or expired signed cursor returns HTTP 400:

```json theme={"theme":"vitesse-black"}
{
  "error": {
    "type": "invalid_request",
    "message": "Invalid cursor: expired or malformed; restart without cursor",
    "metadata": []
  }
}
```

Changing the query, mode, filters, or API version returns HTTP 400:

```json theme={"theme":"vitesse-black"}
{
  "error": {
    "type": "invalid_request",
    "message": "Invalid cursor: query, mode, filters and API version must remain unchanged",
    "metadata": []
  }
}
```

Restart without `cursor` after these errors. Do not retry the same invalid cursor.

### Other search errors

```json 400 — Unsupported field theme={"theme":"vitesse-black"}
{
    "error": {
        "type": "invalid_request",
        "message": "Unsupported columns in conditions: ['nonexistent_field']",
        "metadata": []
    }
}
```

```json 400 — Invalid operator theme={"theme":"vitesse-black"}
{
    "error": {
        "type": "invalid_request",
        "message": "'filters.type' must be one of: =, !=, <, =<, >, =>, in, not_in, contains, not_contains, is_null, is_not_null, (.), [.]. Got '>='.",
        "metadata": [
            {
                "field": "filters.type",
                "type": "enum",
                "message": "'filters.type' must be one of: =, !=, <, =<, >, =>, in, not_in, contains, not_contains, is_null, is_not_null, (.), [.]. Got '>='."
            }
        ]
    }
}
```

> [!NOTE]
>
> Use `=>` for greater-than-or-equal and `=<` for less-than-or-equal. The operators `>=` and `<=` are not supported.

```json 401 — Invalid API key theme={"theme":"vitesse-black"}
{
    "error": {
        "type": "unauthorized",
        "message": "Invalid API key in request.",
        "metadata": []
    }
}
```

***

## API reference summary

| Detail | Value |
| - | - |
| **Endpoint** | `POST /company/search` |
| **Auth** | Bearer token + `x-api-version: 2025-11-01` |
| **Request** | `filters`, `search`, `fields`, `sorts`, `limit`, `cursor` |
| **Response** | `{ companies, next_cursor, total_count }` |
| **Pagination** | Cursor-based for both filter-only and ranked search; ranked pages have a 100-result maximum. |
| **Empty result** | `200` with `"companies": []` |
| **Errors** | `400` (bad field/operator), `401` (bad auth), `403` (permission/credits), `500` (server error) |

## How sorts work

The `sorts` parameter orders your results. Each sort rule needs:

* **`column`** — a dot-path field (e.g., `funding.total_investment_usd`, `headcount.total`, `basic_info.name`).
* **`order`** — either `asc` (ascending) or `desc` (descending).

You can provide multiple sort rules. The API applies them in order. For the
full list of sortable fields, see
[Search reference](/company-docs/search/reference#searchable-fields).

`sorts` is not supported with ranked `search`. Ranked results are ordered by
relevance.

***

## Paginate through results

### Ranked pagination

For `hybrid`, `lexical`, and `semantic` search, pass the previous response's
`next_cursor` as `cursor`. Each page accepts `limit` from 1 to 100 (default 20).
A search covers at most 1,000 candidate positions. `total_count` is always `null`;
it does not report the candidate ceiling or the total matching population.

* Keep `search.query`, `search.mode`, `filters`, and `x-api-version` unchanged.
* You may change `limit` and authorized `fields` between pages.
* Do not send `sorts` with ranked search.
* Cursors expire 20 minutes after the initial search. Paging does not renew them.
* The first 100 candidates are reranked. Later candidates use retrieval ranking
  without another reranking pass.
* Candidate order is retained, but company records are read again for each page.
  Deleted companies or records that no longer satisfy filters are omitted and
  still consume their original positions. A short or empty page can have a cursor.
* Continue until `next_cursor` is `null`. A cursor does not guarantee a nonempty next page.
* If the cursor expires, cached results are unavailable, or the search index changes,
  restart without `cursor`.

See the [worked request and response](/company-docs/search/introduction#examples).

### Filter-only pagination

When your search matches more companies than your `limit`, use cursor-based pagination to walk through all pages.

**First page:** send your normal search request.

```bash First page theme={"theme":"vitesse-black"}
curl --request POST \
  --url https://api.crustdata.com/company/search \
  --header 'authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY' \
  --header 'content-type: application/json' \
  --header 'x-api-version: 2025-11-01' \
  --data '{
    "filters": {
      "field": "locations.country",
      "type": "in",
      "value": ["USA"]
    },
    "sorts": [{"field": "crustdata_company_id", "order": "asc"}],
    "limit": 100,
    "fields": [
      "crustdata_company_id",
      "basic_info.name",
      "basic_info.primary_domain"
    ]
  }'
```

**Next page:** take the `next_cursor` value from the response and pass it in your next request. Keep the same `filters`, `sorts`, `limit`, and `fields`.

```bash Next page theme={"theme":"vitesse-black"}
curl --request POST \
  --url https://api.crustdata.com/company/search \
  --header 'authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY' \
  --header 'content-type: application/json' \
  --header 'x-api-version: 2025-11-01' \
  --data '{
    "filters": {
      "field": "locations.country",
      "type": "in",
      "value": ["USA"]
    },
    "sorts": [{"field": "crustdata_company_id", "order": "asc"}],
    "limit": 100,
    "fields": [
      "crustdata_company_id",
      "basic_info.name",
      "basic_info.primary_domain"
    ],
    "cursor": "PASTE_NEXT_CURSOR_VALUE_HERE"
  }'
```

Continue until `next_cursor` is `null`, which means you have reached the last page.

> [!WARNING]
>
> Changing `filters`, `sorts`, or `fields` between pages invalidates the
> cursor. Always include `sorts` when paginating to guarantee stable ordering.

See the [full API reference](/openapi-specs/2025-11-01/introduction) for the complete OpenAPI schema.


# Data Export
Source: https://docs.crustdata.com/export-docs/data-export

Export every person or company matching a search as a scheduled CSV or JSONL file, with the columns you pick, straight from the Crustdata dashboard.

Export everyone who matches a search as a file, once or on a schedule.

Data Export lives in the dashboard at
[app.crustdata.com/data-exports](https://app.crustdata.com/data-exports). There
is no API for it.

## Create an export

**1. Pick People or Companies**

Fixed once you save.

**2. Choose the filter**

Pick a template, or describe your own in plain English.

![Template cards and the Describe your own box](https://mintcdn.com/crustdata/alqB64hx4VtFTD-6/images/data-export/query.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=alqB64hx4VtFTD-6\&q=85\&s=f873bcd19dd6bb10e83f3f25b1085515)

**Describe a change** refines it. **Edit the query** opens the raw JSON.

**3. Choose the columns**

One column per field, with a recommended set already selected.

![The column picker with the Current employment group open](https://mintcdn.com/crustdata/alqB64hx4VtFTD-6/images/data-export/columns.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=alqB64hx4VtFTD-6\&q=85\&s=5e2b5953de862769900b574326d2e154)

The picker starts on **Recommended for you**; the link beneath shows every
group. Both list only the fields your team can read. If a saved export's
columns stop being readable, editing it drops them.

**4. Name it, then set size, cadence, and format**

The match count and credit estimate update as you go.

![Name, number of entries, cadence, format, and the credit estimate](https://mintcdn.com/crustdata/alqB64hx4VtFTD-6/images/data-export/schedule.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=alqB64hx4VtFTD-6\&q=85\&s=ea61871b178d792415e704fc1a7e8192)

**5. Review and start**

Accept the terms, then **Start export**. The first run starts immediately.

![The review summary and the columns it will write](https://mintcdn.com/crustdata/alqB64hx4VtFTD-6/images/data-export/review.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=alqB64hx4VtFTD-6\&q=85\&s=08001b5e7734bb20844c33c2f6c7287b)

## Filters

An export filter is the same filter tree that
[Person Search](/person-docs/search/introduction) and
[Company Search](/company-docs/search/introduction) accept.

```json theme={"theme":"vitesse-black"}
{
  "op": "and",
  "conditions": [
    { "field": "taxonomy.categories", "type": "[.]", "value": "FinTech" },
    { "field": "funding.last_round_type", "type": "=", "value": "series_a" }
  ]
}
```

An export rejects natural-language ranking through `search.query` and custom
`sorts`. Sort the file after you download it.

For fields and operators, see the
[Person Search reference](/person-docs/search/reference) and the
[Company Search reference](/company-docs/search/reference).

## Schedules

| Cadence | What happens |
| - | - |
| Once | Runs once, right after you save. |
| Daily | Every day, around this time. |
| Weekly | Every week, same day and time. |
| Monthly | Every month, same day. |

Your rows per run decide which cadences you are offered.

| Rows per run | Cadences available |
| - | - |
| Up to 1,000,000 | Once, Daily, Weekly, Monthly |
| 1,000,001 to 10,000,000 | Once, Weekly, Monthly |
| Over 10,000,000 | Once, Monthly |

* **Run now** triggers an extra run at any time, including on a paused export.
* **Pause schedule** stops future runs. **Resume schedule** waits one full
  period before the next run, so a daily export resumed today runs tomorrow.
* Missed runs are never replayed. An overdue export runs once, then returns to
  its cadence.
* Three failed scheduled runs in a row pause the export.
* Edits apply to the next run. A run in progress keeps the configuration it
  started with.

## Files

Both formats download gzipped.

| Format | Shape |
| - | - |
| CSV | One column per selected field, in selection order. Opens in Excel or Google Sheets. |
| JSONL | One JSON object per line, nested like the API. |

### Lists in CSV

List fields spread across numbered columns named `path[i].leaf`. Selecting
`experience.employment_details.past.title` gives you
`experience.employment_details.past[0].title`,
`experience.employment_details.past[1].title`, and so on. Every row gets as many
slots as the widest row needs.

The list fields are `education.schools` and current and past employment for
people, and `basic_info.all_domains`, `basic_info.markets`, `funding.investors`,
`locations.all_office_addresses`, `revenue.public_markets.stock_symbols`, and
the `taxonomy` lists for companies. Pick JSONL to keep the nesting.

## Limits

* **Rows per run.** Prefilled with 100,000, or your ceiling if that is lower.
  The default ceiling is 1,000,000 and your team's may differ. A search matching
  more rows than your cap still runs, writes up to the cap, and marks the run
  `capped`.
* **Concurrency.** One run at a time per export, two per team. A run that cannot
  start is skipped and recorded, not queued.

Need more than the ceiling? [Contact us](mailto:support@crustdata.co) about a
managed export.

## Runs

Every run lands in the export's history with its status, rows written out of
rows matched, credits, duration, and a download link. Expand a run for its
completion report, which shows how many rows carried a value in each column.

![The run history with a completion report and the export configuration](https://mintcdn.com/crustdata/alqB64hx4VtFTD-6/images/data-export/runs.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=alqB64hx4VtFTD-6\&q=85\&s=33ef756212a334820ee63f9f2f678e02)

| Status | What it means |
| - | - |
| Queued | Accepted, waiting to start. |
| Running | Writing rows now. Cancel it to stop early. |
| Completed | Finished. There is always a file, even when nothing matched. |
| Partial | Stopped early. The file holds the rows written so far. |
| Failed | No file. Costs nothing. |
| Cancelled | You stopped it. The file keeps the rows written so far. |
| Skipped | Never started, so no file and no charge. |

Download links are minted on click and last one hour. Anyone with the link can
download the file.

## Pricing

A run bills per row written, at your plan's
[Person Search](/person-docs/search/introduction) or
[Company Search](/company-docs/search/introduction) rate. Premium filters and
columns add their own per-row charge.

* Previews are free.
* Failed and skipped runs cost nothing.
* A run that stops part-way bills only the rows it wrote.
* If your balance will not cover the first run, you can still save. The run is
  skipped until you top up.

See [Pricing](/general/pricing) for your rate and [Credits](/general/credits) for
your balance.

## When a run does not finish

| What you see | What happened |
| - | - |
| Not enough credits | Your balance would not cover the run. Nothing was charged. |
| Columns no longer permitted | A selected column left your plan. Edit the columns and run again. |
| A run was already in progress | Wait for it, or cancel it. |
| Team already had 2 runs in progress | Try again when one finishes. |
| Timed out | The run exceeded its time limit. |
| Something went wrong on our side | Ours to fix. Contact support if it repeats. |

Running out of credits mid-run stops the run at its next checkpoint, keeps the
rows already written, and bills only those. It shows as `Partial`.

## Roles

| Role | What you can do |
| - | - |
| Admin | Create, edit, run, pause, and delete exports, and download files. |
| Member | View every export and its runs, and download files. No changes. |

## Managed exports

Bulk dumps Crustdata provisions for your team appear under **Managed exports**,
below your own, each with its own run history. They are read only here; to
change one, contact your account manager.

## Terms

Creating an export means accepting the
[Terms of Service](https://crustdata.com/terms) and the
[Data Export Terms](https://app.crustdata.com/terms/data-export): internal use
only, no resale or redistribution, and you handle personal data under the
privacy laws that apply to you.

## What to do next

> **[Person filters](/person-docs/search/reference)**
>
> Every field and operator an export filter accepts.

> **[Company filters](/company-docs/search/reference)**
>
> The same for companies.

> **[Track changes instead](/watcher-docs/person/discovery)**
>
> For only what is new since last time, use a discovery watcher.


# Crustdata CLI
Source: https://docs.crustdata.com/for-agents/cli

Use the Crustdata API from your terminal. Search, identify, and enrich companies and people, run bulk jobs, and get raw JSON for scripts and agents.

The `crustdata` CLI gives you the full Crustdata API in your terminal. Each API endpoint is a command with typed flags. On a terminal, the CLI prints markdown tables. When you pipe the output to another program, the CLI prints raw JSON. You, your scripts, and your agents can use the same commands.

## Quick start

**1. Install**

On macOS and Linux:

```bash theme={"theme":"vitesse-black"}
curl -fsSL https://static-assets.crustdata.com/cli/install.sh | sh
```

On Windows:

```powershell theme={"theme":"vitesse-black"}
irm https://static-assets.crustdata.com/cli/install.ps1 | iex
```

The installer verifies the checksums and puts the binary in `~/.crustdata/bin`. It also adds that directory to your `PATH`. To stop the installer from changing your `PATH`, set `CRUSTDATA_NO_MODIFY_PATH=1`.

After the install, open a new terminal. To upgrade the CLI later, run `crustdata upgrade`.

**2. Authenticate**

```bash theme={"theme":"vitesse-black"}
crustdata auth login
```

This command opens your browser. Sign in and pick your team. The CLI then saves the API key for that team.

If the machine has no browser, add `--no-browser`. The CLI prints the sign-in URL and asks you to paste the redirect back.

For CI and scripts, set `CRUSTDATA_API_KEY`, or read the key from a file with `crustdata auth login --with-token < key.txt`. [Non-interactive authentication](#non-interactive-authentication) compares the options.

**3. Run a command**

```bash theme={"theme":"vitesse-black"}
crustdata company enrich --domains stripe.com --fields basic_info,headcount
```

This command returns the `basic_info` and `headcount` fields for `stripe.com`.

## Commands

Run `crustdata <command> --help` to see the flags and runnable examples for any command.

| Command | What it does |
| - | - |
| `company search / identify / enrich / reviews / suggest` | Finds, identifies, and enriches companies. Gets employee reviews. Suggests values for search fields. |
| `person search / enrich / contacts / dev / suggest` | Finds and enriches people. Gets contact details and dev-platform profiles. Suggests values for search fields. |
| `job search / suggest` | Searches job listings. Suggests values for search fields. |
| `social-post search / fetch` | Finds social posts by keyword, person, or company. |
| `web search / fetch` | Searches the web and fetches pages in real time. |
| `batch <noun> <verb>` | Runs bulk jobs. It submits a job, waits for it with `--wait`, and downloads the JSONL results. |
| `account credits / endpoints` | Shows your credit balance and rate limits. |
| `auth login / logout / status / token` | Manages authentication with browser sign-in or an API key. |
| `docs / docs read / docs fs` | Searches and reads these docs from the terminal. |
| `mcp install / list / remove` | Installs, lists, and removes the Crustdata MCP server in agent clients. |
| `upgrade` | Updates the CLI in place and verifies the checksum. |

### Live mode

Four commands support `--live`:

* `company search`
* `person search`
* `person enrich`
* `job search`

Without `--live`, these commands query the indexed dataset. With `--live`, they query the professional network in real time.

Live search uses different field names from indexed search, for example `REGION` and `CURRENT_TITLE`. Live `company search` and live `person search` also need `--page`.

## Filters

Search commands take a `--filter` flag in the form `'field op value'`. You can repeat `--filter`. The CLI joins all filters with AND.

```bash theme={"theme":"vitesse-black"}
crustdata company search \
  --filter 'headcount.total > 100' \
  --filter 'locations.country in United States,Canada' \
  --limit 25
```

The operators are the same as in the API: `=`, `!=`, `<`, `>`, `=<`, `=>`, `in`, `not_in`, `(.)`, and `[.]`. For `in` and `not_in`, give a comma-separated list of values.

Field names are the API's dot-paths, such as `headcount.total`. If the API does not know a field name, it returns `invalid_request: Unsupported columns in conditions`. To check a field name before you send a request, use `--dry-run`, tab completion, or the field tables in the API reference.

### OR logic and nested groups

`--filter` gives you AND only. For OR logic and nested groups, write the full JSON request body and pass it with `--input`:

* `--input query.json` reads the body from a file.
* `--input -` reads the body from stdin.

If you also pass a flag, the flag value replaces the matching field in the body. The [company examples](#companies) include an OR query.

## Output

On a terminal, the CLI prints markdown tables. When you pipe the output, the CLI prints the raw JSON response. To choose the format yourself, add `--format json` or `--format md`.

To select part of the JSON response, use the built-in `--jq` flag. You do not need to install `jq`. `--jq` always prints JSON.

```bash theme={"theme":"vitesse-black"}
crustdata account credits --jq .account.credits
```

The CLI writes data only to stdout. It writes progress messages and hints to stderr.

The CLI does not fetch the next page for you, because each page costs credits. To get the next page of an indexed search, pass the `next_cursor` value from the response to `--cursor`.

### Exit codes

| Code | Meaning |
| - | - |
| `0` | The command succeeded. |
| `1` | The command failed because of an API error, a bad flag, or a missing argument. |
| `4` | The command failed because of an authentication error. |

## Preview requests for free

Use these tools to build a request before you spend credits:

* `--dry-run` prints the request body that the CLI composes, and does not send it. Every request command supports `--dry-run`.
* `--example` prints request examples from the API spec. Every request command supports `--example`.
* Tab completion suggests field names and operators.

These tools spend no credits and need no authentication.

### Dry runs

```bash theme={"theme":"vitesse-black"}
# See exactly what --filter compiles into, without sending it
crustdata company search --dry-run \
  --filter 'headcount.total > 10000' \
  --filter 'locations.country in United States' --limit 5

# Live mode composes a flat array instead of a condition tree
crustdata person search --dry-run --live \
  --filter 'CURRENT_TITLE in CEO' --page 1

# See how flags override an --input body
echo '{"limit":100,"cursor":"abc"}' | \
  crustdata company search --input - --limit 5 --dry-run
```

### Spec examples

```bash theme={"theme":"vitesse-black"}
# List the spec's ready-made request bodies
crustdata company search --example

# Print one of them
crustdata company search --example=recently_funded_us_companies

# Use a spec example as the body, add your flags, and preview it
crustdata company search --example=recently_funded_us_companies > /tmp/q.json
crustdata company search --input /tmp/q.json --limit 3 --dry-run
```

> [!NOTE]
>
> To print a named example, use the `=` form: `--example=name`. With no name, `--example` lists the examples that exist.

### Tab completion

To turn on tab completion in your current shell session, run this line:

```bash theme={"theme":"vitesse-black"}
source <(crustdata completion zsh)   # or bash / fish / powershell
```

To turn on completion for every new session, follow the steps in `crustdata completion zsh --help`.

Tab completion then fills in field names and operators:

```bash theme={"theme":"vitesse-black"}
crustdata company search --filter 'head<TAB>      # headcount.* fields from the spec vocabulary
crustdata company search --live --filter '<TAB>   # vocabulary flips to REGION, COMPANY_HEADCOUNT, ...
crustdata company search --filter 'headcount.total <TAB>   # the 10 operators
```

Tab completion does not fill in values. To get valid values for a field, use a `suggest` command, such as `crustdata company suggest country 'Uni'` or `crustdata person suggest basic_profile.city 'San'`. Unlike the tools above, `suggest` calls the API.

## Examples

Each example below runs as written on CLI v0.2.5.

### Companies

```bash theme={"theme":"vitesse-black"}
# Enrich one company
crustdata company enrich --domains stripe.com --fields basic_info,headcount

# Get one value from the enrichment response
crustdata company enrich --domains stripe.com --fields basic_info \
  --jq '.[0].matches[0].company_data.basic_info.name'

# Match a company name to a company record
crustdata company identify --names "Stripe" --exact-match

# Indexed search: the CLI joins the filters with AND
crustdata company search \
  --filter 'headcount.total > 10000' \
  --filter 'locations.country in United States' \
  --limit 2

# OR logic needs a JSON body. Flags still override body fields such as limit.
echo '{"filters":{"op":"or","conditions":[
  {"field":"basic_info.primary_domain","type":"=","value":"stripe.com"},
  {"field":"basic_info.primary_domain","type":"=","value":"openai.com"}
]}}' | crustdata company search --input - --limit 3 --jq .total_count

# Live search: uses live field names and needs --page
crustdata company search --live --filter 'REGION in United States' --page 1

# Employee reviews for a company
crustdata company reviews --crustdata-company-id 631394

# Suggest valid values for a search field
crustdata company suggest country 'Uni'
```

### People

```bash theme={"theme":"vitesse-black"}
# Indexed person search
crustdata person search \
  --filter 'basic_profile.location.country = United States' --limit 2

# Live person search: uses live field names and needs --page
crustdata person search --live \
  --filter 'CURRENT_TITLE in CEO' \
  --filter 'REGION in United States' --page 1

# Enrich a profile
crustdata person enrich \
  --professional-network-profile-urls https://www.linkedin.com/in/dvdhsu/

# Contact details (fields use dotted paths)
crustdata person contacts \
  --professional-network-profile-urls https://www.linkedin.com/in/dvdhsu/ \
  --fields contact.business_emails

# Dev-platform profile from a GitHub URL
crustdata person dev --profile-url https://github.com/rajnandan1

# Suggest values for a person search field
crustdata person suggest basic_profile.city 'San'
```

### Jobs, posts, and the web

```bash theme={"theme":"vitesse-black"}
# Fuzzy-match job titles with the (.) operator
crustdata job search --filter 'job_details.title (.) engineer' --limit 2

# Social posts by keyword (supports OR/AND, up to 6 terms)
crustdata social-post search --keyword 'series B' --limit 2

# A company's recent posts
crustdata social-post fetch --company-domain stripe.com --limit 2

# Search the web in real time
crustdata web search --query 'crustdata'
```

### Account and housekeeping

```bash theme={"theme":"vitesse-black"}
# Credit balance as a bare number
crustdata account credits --jq .account.credits

# Preview a bulk job without spending credits
crustdata batch person contacts \
  --professional-network-profile-urls https://www.linkedin.com/in/dvdhsu/ \
  --fields contact.business_emails --dry-run

# Update the CLI in place
crustdata upgrade
```

## Bulk jobs

```bash theme={"theme":"vitesse-black"}
crustdata batch person enrich --input people.json --wait --download
```

This command does three things:

1. It submits the bulk job.
2. It polls the job until the job completes (`--wait`).
3. It downloads the results as decompressed JSONL (`--download`).

You can also submit a job without `--wait` and come back to it later:

```bash theme={"theme":"vitesse-black"}
crustdata batch status <id>      # check the job
crustdata batch download <id>    # download the results
```

## Search the docs

The CLI can search and read these docs. It uses the public docs MCP server, so you do not need to authenticate.

```bash theme={"theme":"vitesse-black"}
crustdata docs "how do credits work"        # full-text search with page links
crustdata docs read general/rate-limits     # print a whole page
crustdata docs fs -- tree /api-reference    # browse the docs as a filesystem
```

## Set up the Crustdata MCP

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) lets agent clients, such as Claude Code and Cursor, call external tools. `crustdata mcp install` adds the hosted [Crustdata MCP server](/for-agents/mcp) to your agent clients.

```bash theme={"theme":"vitesse-black"}
crustdata mcp install                # interactive picker
crustdata mcp install claude-code    # installs the Crustdata plugin (MCP + skills)
crustdata mcp install cursor windsurf
crustdata mcp list                   # per-client install state and auth mode
crustdata mcp remove cursor          # deletes only the crustdata entry
```

Supported targets:

* `claude-code` installs the Crustdata plugin, which includes the MCP server and skills. To install only the MCP server, add `--mcp-only`.
* `cursor`, `vscode`, and `windsurf` get a `crustdata` entry in the client's MCP config.
* `claude-desktop` connects through the `mcp-remote` bridge.
* `claude-web` gets printed manual steps, because connectors are set at the account level.

The CLI edits only the `crustdata` entry in each client config. It keeps all other entries as they are. To see the exact change without writing it, add `--dry-run`.

By default, each client signs in with OAuth the first time it connects. For headless setups, where nobody can complete a browser sign-in, use one of these flags:

* `--with-key` writes your saved API key into the client config as plain text. The CLI prints a warning when you use it.
* `--with-key=env` writes the reference `${env:CRUSTDATA_API_KEY}` instead of the key itself.

## For scripts and agents

* When you pipe the output, the CLI always prints raw JSON.
* `--jq` works everywhere and needs no other install.
* `--help` on any command shows runnable examples.
* `--dry-run` composes any request without sending it. An agent can use it to explore commands without spending credits.
* The CLI writes data only to stdout. The [exit codes](#exit-codes) tell you what failed.

### Non-interactive authentication

The CLI opens a browser only when it runs on a real terminal. When stdin is a pipe, the CLI never opens a browser. The CLI shows the paste prompt only when you give it no key in another way. This means an agent never waits on a hidden prompt.

Use one of these three methods:

```bash theme={"theme":"vitesse-black"}
# 1. Environment variable: no login step, and nothing is written to disk.
#    Best for short-lived sandboxes. It wins over the config file when both exist.
export CRUSTDATA_API_KEY=cd_xxx

# 2. Stdin: saves the key in the config file and keeps it out of shell history.
echo "$KEY" | crustdata auth login --with-token

# 3. Inline flag: one command, but the key lands in your shell history.
crustdata auth login --token cd_xxx
```

`auth login` checks the key against the API before it saves the key. If the key is not valid, the command exits with code `4`. A bad key fails at setup, not in the middle of a task. To see the current authentication state, run `crustdata auth status`.


# llms.txt
Source: https://docs.crustdata.com/for-agents/llms

A machine-readable index of the Crustdata documentation that AI tools and agents use to read the docs efficiently.

`llms.txt` is a machine-readable index of this documentation, written for large
language models and AI agents. It maps every page to a one-line summary so a
model can pull the right reference directly instead of crawling the whole site.

The docs expose three machine-readable tiers — pick by how much context you have:

| Tier | URL | Size | Use it to |
| - | - | - | - |
| Index | [`/llms.txt`](https://static-assets.crustdata.com/llms.txt) | \~35 KB | Discover pages and pick what to read |
| Page | append `.md` to any docs URL (e.g. [`/general/pricing.md`](/general/pricing.md)) | 5–50 KB each | Fetch exactly the pages you need |
| Full corpus | [`/llms-full.txt`](https://static-assets.crustdata.com/llms-full.txt) | \~1.5 MB | Ingest everything at once (RAG indexing, local search) — larger than most single model contexts by design |

## What's in it

The index groups every page by product area, mirroring this site:

| Section | Contents |
| - | - |
| Getting started | Introduction, Pricing, Rate limits, Credits, and the MCP server |
| Company, Person, Job, Web, Social Post | Each API area's guides and reference |
| Migration guides | Legacy endpoint → current replacement mappings |
| API reference | Every endpoint in the `2025-11-01` version |

## Use it with an AI tool

Give your AI tool or agent the URL `https://static-assets.crustdata.com/llms.txt`
— the complete index, covering everything listed above including the migration
guides and the full API reference. Tools that support the `llms.txt` convention
can also auto-discover `/llms.txt` on the docs domain, but that copy lists only
a subset of pages, so paste the complete index URL when you can. The model
reads the index, then fetches only the pages it needs as Markdown — keeping
answers accurate and context small.

## What to do next

* **Read the index** — open [`llms.txt`](https://static-assets.crustdata.com/llms.txt) to see every page and its summary.
* **Connect an assistant** — the [MCP server](/for-agents/mcp) lets Claude, Cursor, and other clients query Crustdata in natural language.
* **Start from the top** — the [Introduction](/general/introduction) maps the five API areas.


# MCP Server
Source: https://docs.crustdata.com/for-agents/mcp

Connect Crustdata's B2B data platform to Claude and other AI assistants via MCP (Model Context Protocol).

## Quick start

You need a Crustdata account to use the MCP server. [Sign in or create one](https://app.crustdata.com/auth/login).

The endpoint is the same everywhere:

```
https://install.crustdata.com/mcp
```

> **[Add to Claude](https://claude.ai/customize/connectors?modal=add-custom-connector\&connectorName=Crustdata+MCP\&connectorUrl=https%3A%2F%2Finstall.crustdata.com%2Fmcp)**
>
> Opens the **Add custom connector** dialog on claude.ai.

> **[Add to Cursor](https://cursor.com/install-mcp?name=Crustdata\&config=eyJ1cmwiOiAiaHR0cHM6Ly9pbnN0YWxsLmNydXN0ZGF0YS5jb20vbWNwIn0%3D)**
>
> Installs through Cursor's MCP handler.

> **[Add to VS Code](https://vscode.dev/redirect/mcp/install?name=Crustdata\&config=%7B%22type%22%3A%20%22http%22%2C%20%22url%22%3A%20%22https%3A%2F%2Finstall.crustdata.com%2Fmcp%22%7D)**
>
> Registers the server over streamable HTTP.

> **[Add to ChatGPT](https://chatgpt.com/plugins/plugin_asdk_app_6a8cc6dc38ac819198b700b1b4e67fb0)**
>
> Opens the Crustdata listing in the plugin directory.

**Claude**

The **Add to Claude** card does this in one click. To set it up manually:

**1. Open the connector settings**

In Claude, open **Customize**, then **Connectors**, then **Add custom connector**.

**2. Configure the connection**

* **Name:** Crustdata
* **URL:** `https://install.crustdata.com/mcp`

Click **Add** to save.

**3. Connect**

Open the new connector under **Not connected** and click **Connect**, then sign in with your Crustdata account.

Connectors are account-wide. Once you add it, Crustdata is available on claude.ai, Claude Desktop, and mobile.

**Claude Code**

Add the connector from your terminal:

```bash wrap theme={"theme":"vitesse-black"}
claude mcp add --transport http crustdata https://install.crustdata.com/mcp
```

Then sign in: run `/mcp` inside Claude Code and pick **crustdata**.

The [Crustdata plugin](/integrations/claude-plugin) registers this same connector and adds ready-to-run skills, if you want both in one install.

**Codex CLI**

Add the connector from your terminal:

```bash wrap theme={"theme":"vitesse-black"}
codex mcp add crustdata --url https://install.crustdata.com/mcp
```

Codex detects that the server uses OAuth and opens a Crustdata sign-in in your browser. If the sign-in does not open or does not finish, run `codex mcp login crustdata`.

Run `/mcp` inside Codex to confirm **crustdata** is listed.

The [Crustdata plugin for Codex](/integrations/codex) registers this same connector and adds ready-to-run skills, if you want both in one install.

**Antigravity**

Add Crustdata to Antigravity's MCP config and sign in with your Crustdata account. No API key needed.

Antigravity 2.0, the IDE, and the CLI share one config file, `~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json`. Pick the one you use.

> **Antigravity 2.0**
>
> **1. Open the config folder**
>
> In Antigravity 2.0, click **Settings** at the bottom left, then **Customizations**. Under **Installed MCP Servers**, click **Open MCP Config**. This opens the folder that holds `mcp_config.json` (`~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json`) in your file manager, not the file itself.
>
> **2. Add the server**
>
> Open `mcp_config.json` in a text editor. On a new install the file is empty: paste the block below as is. If the file already has an `mcpServers` object, add the `crustdata` entry inside it.
>
> ```json wrap theme={"theme":"vitesse-black"}
> {
>   "mcpServers": {
>     "crustdata": {
>       "serverUrl": "https://install.crustdata.com/mcp"
>     }
>   }
> }
> ```
>
> Use `serverUrl` for remote servers. Some Antigravity versions reject `url` and `httpUrl`. Save the file.
>
> **3. Refresh**
>
> Click the refresh icon next to **Add MCP**. `crustdata` appears with an **Authenticate** button and an `Unauthorized` error. That is expected until you sign in.
>
> **4. Sign in**
>
> Click **Authenticate** and sign in with your Crustdata account in the browser. Copy the authorization code the browser shows, paste it into the field in Antigravity, and click **Submit**. The dot next to `crustdata` turns green when you are connected.

> **Antigravity IDE**
>
> **1. Open the raw config**
>
> Click **…** at the top of the agent side panel, then **MCP Servers**, **Manage MCP Servers**, **View raw config**. This opens `~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json`.
>
> **2. Add the server**
>
> If the file is empty, paste the block below as is. If it already has an `mcpServers` object, add the `crustdata` entry inside it.
>
> ```json wrap theme={"theme":"vitesse-black"}
> {
>   "mcpServers": {
>     "crustdata": {
>       "serverUrl": "https://install.crustdata.com/mcp"
>     }
>   }
> }
> ```
>
> Save the file.
>
> **3. Refresh**
>
> On the **Manage MCP servers** page, click **Refresh**. `crustdata` appears with **Configure** and **Authenticate** buttons and an `Unauthorized` error. That is expected until you sign in.
>
> **4. Sign in**
>
> On the same page, click **Authenticate** next to `crustdata`. Sign in through your browser. If Antigravity asks for an authorization code, paste it and click **Submit**.

> **Antigravity CLI**
>
> **1. Add the server**
>
> Run this in your terminal, not inside an `agy` session.
>
> ```bash wrap theme={"theme":"vitesse-black"}
> agy mcp add crustdata https://install.crustdata.com/mcp
> ```
>
> Run `agy mcp list` to confirm it is listed.
>
> **2. Sign in**
>
> Start `agy` and run `/mcp`. Select `crustdata` with the arrow keys, press **Enter** for its actions, and choose **Authenticate**. Open the URL it shows, sign in, then paste the authorization code back into the CLI.

**Programmatic access**

You can use the same server from your own code: agent frameworks, backend jobs, or anywhere the sign-in flow is not practical. Connect any MCP client to the endpoint and pass your Crustdata API key as a bearer token.

* **Endpoint:** `https://install.crustdata.com/mcp`
* **Header:** `Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY`

For MCP clients that take a JSON config with custom headers:

```json wrap theme={"theme":"vitesse-black"}
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "crustdata": {
      "type": "streamable-http",
      "url": "https://install.crustdata.com/mcp",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" }
    }
  }
}
```

When Crustdata can't answer a request, your assistant may send us a short report through the `feedback` tool, so we can fix the gap. The tool tells the assistant to leave out names, emails, and other personal details. Your client asks you before the first report. Allow the tool once and your client stops asking.

## Check it worked

Ask your assistant:

> How many credits do I have?

A number means you are connected.

If you get no number:

* Restart your client. A mid-session install may not take effect until it does.
* Re-run your client's sign-in step, which is separate from adding the connector.
* In Antigravity, check that the entry uses `serverUrl`, not `url`, and that you pasted the authorization code after **Authenticate**.
* Watch the [setup walkthrough](#setup-walkthrough).

## Try it

Ask for what you want in plain English:

* "Show me AI startups with 100-500 employees"
* "Who are the engineering leaders at Anthropic?"
* "What jobs does Stripe have open right now?"
* "Find the profile for [jane.doe@acme.com](mailto:jane.doe@acme.com)"
* "Get me the email for this person's profile"

A single request can chain steps. "Find AI startups hiring engineers, then get me the founders' emails" runs start to finish without you breaking it up.

## What you can do

> **Companies**
>
> Find and enrich companies by industry, headcount, location, and funding, with full firmographic profiles.

> **People and contacts**
>
> Search people by title, seniority, company, and skills, then enrich profiles with business emails, personal emails, and phone numbers.

> **Jobs**
>
> Search millions of job listings with filters and breakdowns, or pull a company's live openings on demand.

> **Social and web**
>
> Track recent social posts by person, company, or keyword, and search and read content from across the web.

Hand it a list instead of one name and it enriches the whole list, splitting the work into batches on its own.

## Credits

Every request reports the exact credits it spent, in real time, measured from what the request actually did rather than estimated. Enrichment takes the cheapest correct path, so you do not over-spend by accident.

Costs vary by request and plan. See [Pricing](/general/pricing) for per-request costs and [Rate limits](/general/rate-limits) for limits.

## Catalog resources

The server publishes its own usage guide as MCP resources: markdown pages an agent reads directly instead of re-deriving the tool list and schemas each session. Read `crustdata://catalog` first. It carries the must-know rules and an index of the sections.

| Resource | What's in it |
| - | - |
| `crustdata://catalog` | Start here. The must-know rules and an index of the sections below |
| `crustdata://catalog/quickstart` | How to drive the server: writing a script that composes tool calls |
| `crustdata://catalog/tools` | Every callable tool with its one-line purpose and cost |
| `crustdata://catalog/query-builder` | Filters, operators, and matching behavior |
| `crustdata://catalog/results` | Shaping results: `project`, `compact`, `paginate`, `parallelMap` |
| `crustdata://catalog/fields` | Common filter columns and identifiers per tool |
| `crustdata://catalog/patterns` | Recipes: search then enrich, identify then enrich, bulk, pagination |
| `crustdata://catalog/dry-run` | Testing a script for zero credits before running it for real |
| `crustdata://catalog/ranking` | Bounding result pages server-side and ranking in code |
| `crustdata://catalog/cost` | Credit pricing and the cheapest-path rules |
| `crustdata://catalog/full` | The entire guide in one read |

Any MCP client can fetch these with a standard resource read: `session.read_resource("crustdata://catalog")` in the Python SDK, or `client.readResource({ uri: "crustdata://catalog" })` in TypeScript.

# Capabilities
Source: https://docs.crustdata.com/general/capabilities

What the Crustdata API can do, organized by use case: prospect lists, candidate sourcing, enrichment, job-change and funding alerts, company research, and B2B data for AI agents.

The Crustdata API finds, enriches and monitors people and companies, and searches job postings, social posts and the web. It combines 15+ sources into one record per person or company. Some endpoints are add-ons or in beta; [Permissions](/general/permissions) shows which ones your account can call.

## Build a prospect list from a description of your customer

Describe the accounts and people you want in plain English or with structured filters. Company Search finds the accounts by industry, headcount, funding, location and tech stack. People Search finds the decision-makers inside them by title, seniority and function. Contact Enrichment then returns business emails, personal emails and phone numbers for the people you keep.

Endpoints: [Company Search API](/company-docs/search/introduction), [People Search API](/person-docs/search/introduction), [Semantic People Search API](/guides/person-semantic-search) (beta), [Contact Enrichment API](/person-docs/contact/enrich)

## Source candidates for a recruiting product

Search people by role, skills, location, employer and education, and get each profile back with full work history including start and end dates. Job Title Normalization maps raw job titles to a standard taxonomy so you can rank candidates consistently.

Endpoints: [People Search API](/person-docs/search/introduction), [Job Title Normalization](/guides/job-title-normalization)

## Enrich records you already have

Person Enrichment turns a profile URL into the full person record. Reverse Email Lookup resolves an email address, business or personal, to the person behind it. Company Identify matches a company name, domain or profile URL to a Crustdata company, which Company Enrichment expands into a full profile. On enterprise plans, Batch Person and Company Enrichment take up to 10,000 records per job and deliver the results as a file.

Endpoints: [Person Enrichment API](/person-docs/enrichment/introduction), [Reverse Email Lookup API](/person-docs/contact/identify), [Company Identify API](/company-docs/identify/introduction), [Company Enrichment API](/company-docs/enrichment/introduction), [Batch Person Enrichment API](/person-docs/enrichment/batch-enrich), [Batch Company Enrichment API](/company-docs/enrichment/batch)

## Get alerts on job changes, hiring and funding

Watchers turn a list or a search into a recurring feed. A Person Entity Watcher takes a list of candidates or customers and tells you when one changes jobs or titles. A Company Entity Watcher tracks your accounts for headcount moves, funding rounds and news. Discovery Watchers re-run a saved search and send the people or companies that newly match it. A Job Watcher sends newly posted roles that match your filters. Alerts go to a webhook, Slack or email.

Endpoints: [Person Entity Watcher](/watcher-docs/person/entity), [Company Entity Watcher](/watcher-docs/company/entity), [Person Discovery Watcher](/watcher-docs/person/discovery), [Company Discovery Watcher](/watcher-docs/company/discovery), [Job Watcher](/watcher-docs/job/watch)

## Research a company and its tech stack

Company Enrichment returns firmographics, headcount, funding, revenue, hiring, web traffic, employee reviews and news in one call. Technographics adds the tools and platforms a company uses, detected from its web presence and its job postings. The Job Postings Search API shows what a company is hiring for, and its aggregations count postings by role, location or source.

Endpoints: [Company Enrichment API](/company-docs/enrichment/introduction), [Technographics](/guides/technographics), [Job Postings Search API](/job-docs/search/introduction)

## Track what people and companies post

Social Post Search finds posts by keyword, author, engagement, reactors and mentions. Use it to spot buying intent or to see who engages with a competitor's posts. A Social Post Watcher sends new posts that match your filters.

Endpoints: [Social Post Search API](/social-post-docs/indexed-search/introduction), [Social Post Watcher](/watcher-docs/social-post/discovery)

## Give an AI agent B2B data

Connect Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor or your own agent to Crustdata through the MCP Server, the Crustdata CLI, or the Claude Code and Codex plugins. The agent calls the same search and enrichment endpoints, and uses Web Search and Web Fetch to read news, research papers and any public page.

Endpoints: [MCP Server](/for-agents/mcp), [Crustdata CLI](/for-agents/cli), [Claude Code plugin](/integrations/claude-plugin), [Codex plugin](/integrations/codex), [Web Search API](/web-docs/search/introduction), [Web Fetch API](/web-docs/fetch/introduction)
